slides: Let's continue with the special cases, and look at circular tracks.

slides.say: Now circular tracks. Two runners start together from the same point, and run in the same direction.
The fast one pulls away. Then it chases the slow one from behind, all the way around.
They meet again when the fast one has gained one full lap.
That's a chase, so we subtract the speeds. Imagine the slow one stands still. Then the fast one moves at the difference, and it needs one lap.
at: That's a chase, so we subtract

slides.say: Now a new example. The track is six hundred meters, and the speeds are ten and seven kilometers per hour. Ten minus seven is three.
Six hundred meters is zero point six kilometers.
at: Six hundred meters is zero point six

slides.say: Three kilometers take sixty minutes. Zero point six is a fifth of three, so it takes a fifth of sixty minutes, twelve minutes.
So they meet every twelve minutes.
Now a second example, from a real exam. Car B is twice as fast as car A, in the same direction. Where do they meet first?
at: Car B is twice as fast

slides.say: They meet when B has gained one lap. B covers twice what A covers. So when A has done one lap, B has done two.
at: So when A has done one lap

slides.say: A is back at the start after one lap. So they meet at the start.
at: So they meet at the start

slides.say: Now the runners start together, but run in opposite directions. They run toward each other around the track.
They meet when together they have covered one full lap.
They move toward each other, so we add the speeds.
Now a new example. The track is six hundred meters, and the speeds are ten and eight kilometers per hour. Ten plus eight is eighteen.
Eighteen kilometers take sixty minutes. Zero point six is eighteen divided by thirty. So the time is sixty divided by thirty, two minutes.
Another example. A one-kilometer track, with speeds seven and five. Seven plus five is twelve.
Twelve kilometers take sixty minutes. So one kilometer takes sixty divided by twelve, five minutes.
at: one kilometer takes sixty divided by twelve

slides.say: So let's sum it up. A train passing a post covers its own length. A bridge, a platform or a tunnel means its length plus the train.
On a circular track in the same direction, we subtract the speeds. They meet once every lap the fast one gains.
In opposite directions, we add the speeds. They meet once every lap they cover together.

slides: Take a moment to memorize this. Now try the next question, and I'll see you in the next video.
